articles.title: India's first hydrogen train completes 120 kmph trials, regular speed to rise to 110 kmph
articles.content: News National India’s first hydrogen train completes 120 kmph trials, regular speed to rise to 110 kmph India’s first hydrogen train completes 120 kmph trials, regular speed to rise to 110 kmph Indian Railways is working to increase the regular operating speed of the country’s first hydrogen-powered train to 110 kmph after successfully completing trials at speeds of up to 120 kmph, Railway Board Chairman and CEO Satish Kumar said on Sunday, September 6. Advertisement India TodayNE Sep 07, 2026 , Updated Sep 07, 2026, 8:58 AM IST Follow us: Indian Railways is working to increase the regular operating speed of the country’s first hydrogen-powered train to 110 kmph after successfully completing trials at speeds of up to 120 kmph, Railway Board Chairman and CEO Satish Kumar said on Sunday, September 6. The hydrogen-powered train is currently being operated at a maximum speed of 75 kmph. Kumar said the Railways has completed speed trials at 120 kmph and is now working towards raising its operational speed to 110 kmph. “The operational speed of the hydrogen train has so far been kept at 75 kmph. However, trials have been completed for a speed of 120 kmph. After that, efforts are now underway to operate it at a maximum speed of 110 kmph,” Kumar told reporters in Indore. The Railway Board chairman also said the Railways was holding discussions with various stakeholders to identify suitable routes for deploying hydrogen-powered trains. According to Kumar, the Railways is assessing the infrastructure and operational requirements for running such trains, including arrangements to ensure a reliable supply of hydrogen fuel along the selected routes. Prime Minister Narendra Modi flagged off India’s first hydrogen-powered train on July 17. The train is currently operating on the 89-km Jind-Sonipat route in Haryana. Hydrogen-powered trains differ from conventional diesel trains in that they generate electricity onboard through a fuel-cell system using hydrogen and oxygen. Water vapour and heat are released as by-products of the process. The technology does not involve conventional combustion and eliminates tailpipe emissions associated with diesel-powered trains. Hydrogen-powered trains are therefore being explored as a cleaner alternative for railway routes that are not yet electrified. The Railways’ move to raise the operating speed to 110 kmph is part of efforts to improve the operational performance of hydrogen-powered trains while assessing their potential deployment on other suitable non-electrified routes. articles.title: EOS-05 Completes First Orbit-Raising Manoeuvre - Deccan Chronicle
articles.content: Nellore: India’s latest Earth observation satellite EOS-05 has successfully completed its first orbit-raising manoeuvre, marking a crucial step towards reaching its designated geosynchronous orbit (GSO) at 85.5° East. The manoeuvre was carried out on September 5 at 8.19 p.m., with the satellite’s Liquid Apogee Motor (LAM) firing for 5,406.4 seconds. Following the manoeuvre, the satellite is estimated to be in an orbit of 20,000 km × 31,129 km. ISRO said further orbit-raising manoeuvres would be conducted in the coming days to place EOS-05 in its operational orbit. EOS-05 was launched aboard GSLV-F17 from Sriharikota on September 4 and injected into a sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit (Sub-GTO). ISRO describes it as a state-of-the-art Earth observation spacecraft and India’s first imaging satellite designed to operate from geosynchronous orbit. The GSLV-F17 placed EOS-05 at an apogee of around 31,000 km, higher than the planned 29,000 km, reducing the propulsion work required. Its perigee was around 171 km. Weighing 2,367 kg, EOS-05 is the heaviest satellite launched by a GSLV so far. Once positioned in geosynchronous orbit, it is expected to provide high-frequency Earth imaging and continuous monitoring of large geographical regions. The satellite has an operational life of about nine years, according to ISRO Chairman V. Narayanan. ISRO plans additional orbit-raising manoeuvres to position EOS-05 in its final orbit, around 36,000 km above Earth.

articles.title: ISRO dismisses reports of privatisation as 'completely baseless and incorrect'
articles.content: Nine employee associations representing personnel across ISRO centres and units have sought a written clarification on the future of the agency’s launch vehicle, satellite and operational functions. | X/@isro Subscribe to Notifications Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) on Sunday categorically rejected reports of its privatisation, calling the assertions “completely baseless and incorrect”. ISRO’s response came after service associations representing employees of the agency’s various centres and units had written to its chief, seeking clarification over reports of a proposal to allow private players in the space agency’s manufacturing and operational work. “These assertions are completely baseless and incorrect. We wish to categorically state that ISRO will neither be privatised nor will its importance be diminished,” the space agency said in a lengthy statement posted on X. ISRO further clarified that it will continue to remain India’s principal institution for “advanced space research and technology development, national and strategic missions, space science and exploration, and critical and frontier space capabilities.” However, the agency didn’t completely rule out private-sector participation in space but added the move would not reduce its own role but instead allow it to focus on the future space programmes. “What is changing is not the importance of ISRO, but the scale and structure of India’s space ecosystem,” the statement added. Read ISRO’s full statement on privatisation claims below Earlier this week, service associations representing employees of various Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) centres and units had written to the Department of Space Secretary and ISRO Chairman V Narayanan, seeking official clarification on the government’s policy regarding the privatisation or transfer of ISRO’s manufacturing and operational functions. In a joint representation dated September 4, 2026, nine associations, including the ISRO Staff Association, SHAR Employees Association, ISAC Employees Association, ISRO Staff Association LPSC, ISRO Staff Association-BBU, NRSA Employees Union, Space Employees Association-BBU, ISRO Staff Association-IPRC and SAC Employees Welfare Association, raised concerns over reports and public statements regarding the proposed transfer of various activities from ISRO to private entities and public sector undertakings. The associations cited public statements made by Pawan Kumar Goenka, Chairman of IN-SPACe, at the Summit on August 21, 2026. He was reported to have said: “Eventually, ISRO will not make any launch vehicles and will not manufacture any launch vehicles. That will all be done by the private sector or PSU.” The letter also noted reports that: Transfer has begun with SSLV technology and production rights handed to Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) and is proposed to be extended to PSLV and LVM3; Public sector undertakings may be excluded from the forthcoming transfer process; Routine satellite manufacturing is also to move out of ISRO; Operation of new launch infrastructure, including the Space Launch Complex at Kulasekarapattinam, is being opened to private entities; About 120 technologies have already been transferred from ISRO to the private sector.
